newsitem.title: UK: London should prosper inside EMU or out, study shows.
newsitem.headline: London should prosper inside EMU or out, study shows.

text.p: London will continue to prosper as a global financial centre whether or not Britain decides to participate in a single European currency, the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said.

But in a report pulished on Tuesday, the association warned that Britain could face discrimination if it opted out of joining the currency, to be known as the euro, and might enjoy fewer of the benefits that could result.
"Overall, provided that thorough preparations are put in hand, the UK financial sector should continue to prosper regardless of participation in monetary union," the BBA said.

"London would be strongly placed to attract euro business across a broad range of markets if the UK participates in monetary union. In the event of non-participation, UK markets would still attract considerable euro business."
Its study concluded that if monetary union was dominated by a "high-regulation culture," London's competitive position could be strengthened.

But it added: "Should monetary union prove to be an economic success, London would probably be less favourably positioned to take advantage of the considerable business opportunities that would be likely to ensue."
The study, "Preparing for EMU," was written by a working group established by the BBA, the Association for Payment Clearing Services and the London Investment Banking Association.
Its findings largely echoed remarks last week by Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who said EMU offered "an absolutely huge opportunity" for London.

The study said that while British business leaders had long been sceptical about EMU starting on schedule from 1999, there was now a general recognition that it would probaby start then, or soon afterwards.
The City of London therefore had no room for complacency about its key role as a world financial centre and needed to prepare properly and in good time.

The Bankers' Association urged the government to take a more active role in preparing Britain for the consequences of monetary union and warned that a loss of British influence in the 15-nation bloc could be damaging.
Britain's ruling Conservatives are deeply divided between pro-Europeans such as finance minister Kenneth Clarke and "Euro-sceptics" within the cabinet and on the back-benches of the House of Commons.
"Any serious perception of a UK 'sidelined' in the EU may discourage institutions from basing new operations in the UK," the Bankers' Association said.
"If the UK does not join the single currency, it would be important for the UK to maintain a constructive relationship with participating member states."
It acknowledged that there was a possibility that banks in in non-participating states could face discrimination, such as restricted access to payments facilities developed for the single currency.
However, as payments systems were an integral part of the existing EU single market, restrictions on access could not be justified.
